claims.claim: 100 lookups a second: with lookups this cheap, one process should easily keep up
claims.about: Python Flask, one process with a thread pool (waitress)
claims.measured: python-flask-gthread on 1 CPU: 4,031 req/s plaintext, 3,777 req/s JSON (python-flask sync: about 1,700 req/s)
claims.why: Threaded Flask in one process measured dozens of times above 100 req/s, so 'easily keeps up' fits, even though waitress itself was not benchmarked.

claims.claim: Lookups are binary searches, so one process handles hundreds of requests a second
claims.measured: python-flask-gthread: about 3,800–4,000 req/s on 1 CPU; python-flask: about 1,700 req/s
claims.why: This is a lower bound, and the measured throughput of one Flask process is well above hundreds per second.

claims.claim: Under 50 ms: each lookup is a binary search, so the service meets the 50 ms target
claims.measured: python-flask-gthread at 64 connections and full load: p50 14.72 ms, p99 37.24 ms plaintext; p99 37.73 ms JSON
claims.why: Even at about 4,000 req/s the measured Flask p99 stays under 50 ms, so it should at 100 req/s too, as long as the lookup itself is cheap.

claims.claim: Each lookup should take well under a millisecond (microseconds for the binary search)
claims.why: The benchmarks measure web frameworks, not NumPy binary search over the team's index.

claims.claim: The server starts listening straight away while the index loads in the background
claims.measured: Flask start-up 606–996 ms (python-flask-gthread 606 ms, python-flask 996 ms)
claims.why: Flask measured under about 1 s to start, which counts as straight away next to the 3-minute index load.
